chief_complaint: sudden excruciating pain in my right big toe
hpi_details: 55M presents with acute onset of severe pain, redness, and swelling in his right big toe that started at 3 AM. He cannot bear the weight of a bedsheet on it. He attended a steak and beer dinner last night.

core_concepts: Monosodium urate crystal deposition causing acute monoarthritis, often at the first MTP joint (podagra).
Triggers include alcohol, purine-rich foods, and thiazide diuretics.
common_misconceptions: Assuming urate-lowering therapy must never be started during a flare; when it is indicated, it can be initiated with anti-inflammatory treatment.
dangerous_errors: Missing a septic joint (must tap if diagnosis is uncertain or if fever is present).
management_principles: For an acute flare, a clinician chooses an NSAID, colchicine, or glucocorticoid based on renal function, bleeding/ulcer risk, cardiovascular disease, infection, and drug interactions. Review diuretic therapy with the prescriber rather than stopping it independently; consider urate-lowering therapy for appropriate recurrent/high-risk disease.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Clinical Guidance

reference_soap.subjective: 55M with acute, severe, spontaneous right first MTP pain and redness.
reference_soap.objective: Right 1st MTP is erythematous, swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm the diagnosis with aspiration/crystal analysis when uncertain and send culture urgently if fever or septic arthritis is possible. A clinician should select flare therapy after renal, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and interaction review. Counsel on alcohol/trigger reduction and arrange follow-up to review hydrochlorothiazide with the prescribing clinician and assess need for urate-lowering therapy.

learning_objectives: Identify the classic presentation of acute gout and its triggers.

teaching.one_liner: Acute, exquisite monoarticular pain at the first MTP joint following dietary triggers.

must_ask.say: Did this wake you up suddenly at night with a burning pain?
Did you eat a lot of red meat or drink alcohol before this started?
Is the toe so tender that even a bedsheet touching it is painful?
Are you taking a water pill like hydrochlorothiazide for your blood pressure?
Have you had a fever, and has this happened to you before?

history.answer: My right big toe started throbbing with agonizing pain in the middle of the night, and now it's bright red and terribly swollen.
It is only in my right big toe at the base joint. None of my other toes or joints hurt.
It woke me up out of nowhere around 3 AM today. It reached this peak, unbearable intensity within just a couple of hours.
It is a burning, excruciating, throbbing pain, easily a 10 out of 10. It feels like my toe is stuck in a vice.
Yes, the base of the toe is puffed up like a balloon, bright red, and feels hot like an oven.
I couldn't sleep because of the pain, but it doesn't feel like morning stiffness that loosens up with movement. It just constantly hurts.
Any movement or bumping makes it scream. Even resting a light bedsheet on top of the toe felt unbearable.
I cannot put any weight on that foot at all. I had to hop on my left leg and hobble on my right heel to get here.
No, I don't feel feverish, and I haven't had any chills or shivering.
No, I did not stub, twist, or injure my toe, and I didn't hear any pop or crack.
I have never had anything like this happen before. This is the very first time.
I feel completely fine overall, aside from this terrible toe pain. No extreme tiredness or unintentional weight loss.
No rashes, no scalp flakes, no mouth sores, and my eyes aren't red or gritty.
No, my back and heels feel fine, and my other fingers and toes are not swollen.
No, no stomach bugs, diarrhea, burning when I urinate, or recent sore throats.
I went out for a heavy steak dinner and drank about four or five pints of beer last night. Also, I take a water pill every morning for blood pressure.
No, I have never taken steroid pills, never had joint injections, and I do not have artificial joints.
I have been happily married for twenty-five years with no outside sexual contacts.
I honestly thought I somehow broke my toe in my sleep without realizing it.
I am worried this might cause permanent joint damage or keep me from walking properly.
I really need some strong pain relief right away because I can barely stand this.
I have had high blood pressure for about five years, but no other health issues.
No prior surgeries or hospital admissions.
I take hydrochlorothiazide 25 milligrams once daily for my high blood pressure. I don't take any other regular medicines or supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I usually have two or three beers most evenings, and more on weekends or when dining out with friends.
I work as an office manager and live with my wife in an apartment.
My father had high blood pressure and also suffered from gout attacks in his feet, but no rheumatoid arthritis in the family.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Middle-aged male sitting uncomfortably, holding his bare right foot elevated and guarding it closely from touching anything.

Right first metatarsophalangeal joint is markedly swollen, erythematous, warm to the touch, and exquisitely tender with severely restricted range of motion; other joints in both upper and lower extremities are normal without swelling, warmth, or deformity.
Erythematous, tense, shiny skin over the right first metatarsophalangeal joint without ulceration or fluctuance; no visible tophi, nodules, or psoriatic plaques on ears, elbows, or elsewhere.
Severe antalgic gait with complete refusal to bear weight on the medial right forefoot, hobbling cautiously on the heel.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily palpable and symmetric bilaterally with capillary refill under 2 seconds.
